name: Hydroxyapatite cement forehead contouring

lead: Hydroxyapatite cement is a calcium-phosphate paste that sets into a bone-like material. Surgeons mold it over the frontal bone to build up a flat or irregular forehead, and in feminisation surgery it is combined with burring down a prominent brow.
The appeal is a customised, permanent contour. Published evidence consists of small case series, including a 21-patient series reporting good aesthetic results, and surgeon technique papers.

paras: The procedure is performed by a surgeon, typically through a scalp incision to expose the bone, where the cement is mixed, shaped and allowed to set. It is sometimes combined with reduction of the brow ridge.
As open cranial surgery it carries general surgical and anaesthetic risks. Cranioplasty literature has reported delayed inflammatory reactions to the cement, per the 2011 series authors.

chain: Smoother, more projected or balanced forehead
angle.text: It changes the forehead's shape itself, adding projection or filling irregularities, and in some protocols is paired with brow-ridge reduction for a rounder profile.

lead: Hydroxyapatite cement (HAC) forehead contouring is a craniofacial procedure in which a moldable calcium-phosphate cement is applied to the frontal bone to alter its shape. Hydroxyapatite is the main mineral of bone, making up roughly 65-70% of bone mass, and is used as a bone filler and implant coating.[1]

Its best-documented cosmetic use is frontal bone remodeling in gender-affirming surgery. A 2011 case series of 21 patients in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery combined burring of the supraorbital ridge and frontal bossing with HAC augmentation through a coronal approach.[2] Cranial vault irregularities are another stated use.[2]
infobox: Coronal scalp incision in the main series[2]

paras: The cement is mixed with sterile water and molded on the bone, setting in about 15 minutes in the 2011 series.[2]

Uses described include feminisation of the forehead, augmentation of a flat or receding forehead and correction of cranial vault irregularities. The 2011 authors present HAC as an alternative to autologous bone, polyethylene and methylmethacrylate, each of which has drawbacks.[2]

The main published series (Hoenig, 2011) followed 21 male-to-female patients for a median of 18 months. Results were rated good to excellent in 15 cases and satisfactory in 2, with stable contours and no reported complications, though assessment was subjective, photographs were scored by two residents, and there was no comparison group.[2] No randomised or comparative trials were located.

The authors of the 2011 series note that other cranioplasty studies, mainly in tumour patients, reported delayed inflammatory reactions with HAC, with unclear cause.[2] Exposing the frontal bone required a coronal incision.

timeline.event: Hoenig publishes 21-patient frontal bone remodeling series.[2]
